query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pre‐formed silicide coating (e.g., a Si–Cr–Fe based coating with a dual-layer structure) on a refractory high-entropy alloy such as MoNbTaTiW will enhance its high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a continuous, protective oxide scale that slows oxygen ingress compared to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-fabricated refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW produced by conventional melting or additive manufacturing) in its uncoated state.
generation.intervention: Deposit a silicide coating using a fused slurry method to produce a dual-layer structure: an outer high-silicon layer (predominantly MSi2) and an inner lower-silicon layer (predominantly M5Si3).
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation testing in air at approximately 900°C for 10 hours (or similar durations that reflect extreme-temperature service conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an adherent, continuous silicide/oxide scale on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The silicide coating reacts at high temperature to form a dense, stable silica-based oxide layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, thereby reducing further oxidation of the underlying refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the coated sample will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and a more intact, less porous oxide layer, indicating improved high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.baseline: The uncoated refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW) when exposed to the same oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold under high-temperature oxidative environments (around 900°C in air for up to 10 hours); behavior outside this specific temperature and time regime or under different atmospheric conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how uniformly the coating adheres over large-scale components, if any deleterious effects on room-temperature mechanical properties occur, or if the coating may spall under thermal cycling; scaling up the coating process may also introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MoNbTaTiW samples: one set coated with the Si–Cr–Fe silicide coating via a fused slurry process, and one set left uncoated. Subject both sets to oxidation in static air at 900°C for 10 hours. Post-exposure, measure the oxidation weight gain, analyze the oxide scale’s continuity and thickness using microscopy (e.g., SEM and EDS), and compare the degree of oxidation between the coated and uncoated samples.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM
Phase composition of the oxide layer via XRD or EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least a ~20% lower oxidation weight gain and a more continuous oxide layer) compared to the uncoated samples under these test conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [,,,,,,]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [,,,,,,]. For example, Mo25Nb25Ta25W25 and Mo20Nb20Ta20W20V20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs []. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [,].
